blocks.text: A healthy 25-year-old volunteer sleeps through the night and is woken at 7 am, ten hours after his last meal. His blood glucose is a normal 4.6 mmol/L, although he has eaten nothing and his brain has been consuming glucose all night. Where did that glucose come from? And if he were to carry on fasting for five weeks, how would his brain keep working without the large daily glucose supply it normally demands?

blocks.markdown: The body does not eat continuously, yet the brain, red blood cells and other tissues need a steady fuel supply. Metabolism therefore alternates between a **fed (absorptive) state**, in which nutrients are stored, and a **fasting (post-absorptive) state**, in which stores are mobilised. The switch between them is controlled mainly by two pancreatic hormones with opposite actions: **insulin** (from beta cells, released when blood glucose rises) and **glucagon** (from alpha cells, released when blood glucose falls). Adrenaline and cortisol support the fasting response.

blocks.title: Fed state and fasting state
blocks.text: In the fed state (roughly 0 to 4 hours after a meal) the insulin to glucagon ratio is high and tissues take up and store fuel as glycogen, triacylglycerol and protein. In the fasting state the ratio is low and the body mobilises glycogen, fat and, later, protein, so that blood glucose is maintained.

rows: Stimulates glycogen synthesis, glycolysis and fatty acid synthesis; suppresses gluconeogenesis and glycogen breakdown
Stimulates glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis; suppresses glycogen synthesis and glycolysis
Promotes glucose uptake (insert GLUT4 transporters), glycogen synthesis and protein synthesis
No effect (muscle lacks glucagon receptors); adrenaline mobilises muscle glycogen for the muscle's own use
Promotes glucose uptake (GLUT4), triacylglycerol synthesis and storage, and lipoprotein lipase; inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase
Activates hormone-sensitive lipase (with adrenaline), releasing fatty acids and glycerol
blocks.caption: Actions of insulin and glucagon on the three main metabolic tissues.

blocks.markdown: **Mechanism in outline.** Insulin acts through a receptor tyrosine kinase and generally promotes dephosphorylation of key enzymes (activating glycogen synthase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase). Glucagon acts through a G protein-coupled receptor, raising cyclic AMP and activating protein kinase A, which phosphorylates enzymes (activating glycogen phosphorylase and hormone-sensitive lipase; inactivating glycogen synthase). The same enzyme is therefore switched in opposite directions by the two hormones, which gives rapid, coordinated control.

blocks.title: Predicting the hormonal switch after a meal
blocks.prompt: A person eats a carbohydrate-rich meal. Predict the changes in insulin and glucagon and the consequences for hepatic glycogen metabolism and adipose lipolysis.

steps.text: Blood glucose rises, so beta cells release insulin and alpha-cell glucagon release falls; the insulin to glucagon ratio is high.
In the liver, insulin activates glycogen synthase (dephosphorylated form) and inhibits glycogen phosphorylase, so glucose is stored as glycogen.
In adipose tissue, insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase and activates lipoprotein lipase, so fat is stored and fatty acid release falls.

blocks.answer: High insulin to glucagon ratio: liver stores glycogen and synthesises fat; adipose lipolysis is suppressed and triacylglycerol is stored.

blocks.markdown:
**How the liver maintains blood glucose between meals.** The liver is the only major organ that releases glucose into blood in significant amounts, because it expresses **glucose-6-phosphatase**, which converts glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose (muscle lacks this enzyme, so muscle glycogen cannot be exported as glucose). The liver uses two sources in sequence:

1. **Glycogenolysis** (from about 1 to 2 hours after a meal): glycogen phosphorylase, activated by glucagon via cyclic AMP, releases glucose-1-phosphate from liver glycogen, which is converted to glucose-6-phosphate and then free glucose. Liver glycogen is limited (of the order of 100 g) and is largely used up within roughly 12 to 24 hours of fasting.
2. **Gluconeogenesis** (increasingly important after about 6 to 12 hours): new glucose is made from **lactate** (from muscle and red cells), **glycerol** (from adipose lipolysis) and **amino acids**, especially alanine, from muscle protein. Even-chain fatty acids cannot be converted to net glucose, because their acetyl-CoA carbons cannot be converted to oxaloacetate in mammals.

The kidney also contributes gluconeogenesis in prolonged fasting.

headers: Main fuel of muscle and liver
rows: Glucose (and stored as glycogen and fat)
Gluconeogenesis (liver and kidney) from amino acids, lactate, glycerol
Fatty acids; ketone body production rising
Mainly ketone bodies (about two thirds of energy), the rest glucose
blocks.caption: Fuel use through feeding, fasting and starvation (times are approximate and vary between people).

blocks.markdown: **The brain in the fed state and in starvation.** In the fed state the brain uses glucose almost exclusively, about 120 g per day in an adult, because fatty acids bound to albumin do not provide fuel for brain cells. In prolonged starvation the liver produces large amounts of **ketone bodies** (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate) from fatty acids. After several days enzymes for ketone body use increase in the brain, and ketone bodies can supply roughly two thirds of its energy, so the brain's glucose requirement falls to about 40 g per day. This **protein-sparing** adaptation reduces the amount of muscle protein that must be broken down for gluconeogenesis and prolongs survival.

blocks.title: Glucose saved by ketone body use
blocks.prompt: A brain that needs 120 g of glucose per day in the fed state needs only 40 g per day after adaptation to starvation. How much glucose per day is saved, and what fraction of the brain's glucose-equivalent energy is now supplied by ketone bodies?

steps.text: Fraction replaced by ketone bodies: the 80 g saved is replaced by ketone body energy, so 80 / 120 is 0.67, about two thirds.
This means the liver has to make far less new glucose from muscle amino acids, so body protein is spared.

blocks.answer: 80 g of glucose per day is saved; ketone bodies provide about two thirds (67 percent) of the brain's energy.

blocks.title: Why muscle glycogen does not raise blood glucose
blocks.text: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so glucose-6-phosphate from muscle glycogen is trapped in the cell and used for the muscle's own glycolysis. Muscle contributes to blood glucose only indirectly, by sending lactate and alanine to the liver.

points: Insulin promotes storage in liver, muscle and adipose tissue; glucagon (acting on liver and adipose tissue) promotes mobilisation.
Between meals the liver maintains blood glucose first by glycogenolysis and then by gluconeogenesis, releasing glucose through glucose-6-phosphatase.
The brain uses glucose in the fed state, and in prolonged starvation uses ketone bodies for about two thirds of its energy, sparing muscle protein.

questions.stem: A student has just eaten a large pasta meal and her blood glucose is rising. What is the effect of the rise in insulin on her liver?

options.text: It stimulates glycogen synthesis and suppresses gluconeogenesis
It stimulates glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis
It stimulates release of free fatty acids from the liver

questions.correctOptionText: It stimulates glycogen synthesis and suppresses gluconeogenesis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: insulin favours storage in the liver and suppresses glucose output.
distractorRationale.b: These are glucagon actions that raise blood glucose.
distractorRationale.c: Ketogenesis is favoured by low insulin and high glucagon.
distractorRationale.d: Insulin inhibits lipolysis (in adipose tissue) and favours fatty acid synthesis in the liver.

questions.explanation: In the fed state, insulin activates glycogen synthase and glycolysis and suppresses gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis in the liver. This stores the glucose load and stops the liver adding more glucose to the blood.

questions.stem: Which pair of effects of insulin on adipose tissue is correct?

options.text: Increases glucose uptake via GLUT4 and inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase
Decreases glucose uptake and activates hormone-sensitive lipase
Increases glucose uptake and activates hormone-sensitive lipase
Decreases glucose uptake and inhibits lipoprotein lipase

questions.correctOptionText: Increases glucose uptake via GLUT4 and inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase

distractorRationale.a: Correct: insulin brings glucose in for triacylglycerol synthesis and blocks fat breakdown.
distractorRationale.b: These effects are the opposite of insulin's actions.
distractorRationale.c: Insulin does not activate hormone-sensitive lipase; it inhibits it.
distractorRationale.d: Insulin increases glucose uptake and activates lipoprotein lipase.

questions.explanation: Insulin inserts GLUT4 transporters into adipocyte membranes, supplying glucose for glycerol-3-phosphate and fatty acid synthesis, and inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase so stored fat is not released. It also increases lipoprotein lipase to deliver fatty acids from lipoproteins.

questions.stem: During a long fast, a runner's blood glucose is maintained at 4 mmol/L. Which statement explains why liver glycogen can release glucose into blood whereas muscle glycogen cannot?

options.text: Liver contains glucose-6-phosphatase, which converts glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose; muscle lacks it
Muscle glycogen is stored as a different polysaccharide

questions.correctOptionText: Liver contains glucose-6-phosphatase, which converts glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose; muscle lacks it

distractorRationale.a: Correct: free glucose can cross the membrane and enter blood, but glucose-6-phosphate cannot.
distractorRationale.b: Muscle has glycogen phosphorylase and uses glycogen for its own glycolysis.

questions.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphatase in the liver removes the phosphate from glucose-6-phosphate, allowing free glucose to leave the cell. Muscle lacks this enzyme, so its glycogen supplies only its own glycolysis.

questions.stem: A patient on a medically supervised fast has been without food for five weeks. Which fuel provides the largest share of the brain's energy?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: after adaptation the brain obtains roughly two thirds of its energy from ketone bodies.
distractorRationale.b: The brain uses glucose almost exclusively only in the fed state.
distractorRationale.c: Fatty acids bound to albumin are not a useful brain fuel.
distractorRationale.d: Amino acids are mainly converted to glucose in the liver rather than burned by the brain.

questions.explanation: In prolonged starvation the liver generates acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, which brain cells learn to oxidise. This lowers the glucose requirement and spares muscle protein.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances cannot be converted to a net amount of glucose by the liver during fasting?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: their acetyl-CoA carbons are lost as CO2 in the citric acid cycle, so no net oxaloacetate is gained.
distractorRationale.b: Lactate is converted to pyruvate and glucose (the Cori cycle).
distractorRationale.c: Glycerol from lipolysis enters gluconeogenesis as dihydroxyacetone phosphate.
distractorRationale.d: Alanine is converted to pyruvate and used for gluconeogenesis.

questions.explanation: Mammals cannot convert acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate, so the carbons of even-chain fatty acids cannot supply net glucose. Lactate, glycerol and amino acids such as alanine are the gluconeogenic substrates.

questions.stem: Which pair of liver actions is stimulated by glucagon during fasting?

options.text: Fatty acid synthesis and glycogen synthesis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: glucagon raises cAMP and activates glycogen phosphorylase and gluconeogenesis.
distractorRationale.b: These are storage pathways favoured by insulin.
distractorRationale.c: Both are storage pathways favoured by insulin.
distractorRationale.d: Both are fed-state pathways favoured by insulin.

questions.explanation: Glucagon raises cyclic AMP in hepatocytes and activates protein kinase A, which activates glycogen phosphorylase and gluconeogenesis and switches off storage pathways. This raises blood glucose between meals.

questions.stem: True or false: during an overnight fast, skeletal muscle glycogen is broken down and the glucose released directly into the blood to maintain blood glucose.
questions.explanation: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so glucose-6-phosphate from its glycogen cannot be converted to free glucose and exported. Blood glucose is maintained by liver glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; muscle contributes only indirectly through lactate and alanine.

questions.stem: After an overnight fast a patient's liver contains 60 g of glycogen. Assume that all of it is converted to blood glucose and that the brain, consuming glucose at 5 g per hour, is the only user. For how many hours could liver glycogen alone supply the brain?
questions.explanation: Duration = amount available / rate of use = 60 g / 5 g per hour = 12 hours. In practice other tissues also use glucose and liver glycogen is depleted sooner, so the liver must switch to gluconeogenesis, which is why glycogen alone cannot maintain blood glucose through a prolonged fast.

questions.stem: Describe the actions of insulin and glucagon on the liver, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, and explain why the two hormones are described as having opposing effects.
markingGuide: Liver, insulin: stimulates glycogen synthesis, glycolysis and fatty acid synthesis; inhibits gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis
Liver, glucagon: stimulates glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis; inhibits glycogen synthesis and glycolysis (via cyclic AMP and protein kinase A)
Muscle: insulin increases GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis and protein synthesis; glucagon has no effect on muscle
Adipose tissue: insulin increases glucose uptake, triacylglycerol storage and lipoprotein lipase and inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase; glucagon (and adrenaline) activates hormone-sensitive lipase
Opposing: the insulin to glucagon ratio sets whether the body is in a storing or a mobilising state, and the same enzymes are switched in opposite directions by dephosphorylation and phosphorylation
questions.explanation: Insulin signals plenty and promotes storage in all three tissues, whereas glucagon signals scarcity and promotes mobilisation, mainly in liver and adipose tissue. Their opposing effects on the phosphorylation state of key enzymes allow tight control of blood glucose.

questions.stem: Explain how the liver maintains blood glucose between meals over the first 24 hours of a fast, and compare the fuels of the brain in the fed state and after five weeks of starvation.
markingGuide: Early fast: glucagon-stimulated glycogenolysis; glucose-6-phosphatase releases free glucose
Liver glycogen is limited (roughly 100 g) and used up within about 12 to 24 hours
Gluconeogenesis takes over from lactate, glycerol and amino acids (such as alanine); even-chain fatty acids cannot give net glucose
Adipose lipolysis supplies fatty acids for muscle and liver and glycerol for gluconeogenesis; the liver forms ketone bodies
Fed state: the brain uses glucose almost exclusively (about 120 g per day)
Prolonged starvation: ketone bodies supply about two thirds of brain energy, glucose need falls (about 40 g per day), sparing muscle protein
questions.explanation: Blood glucose is first maintained by liver glycogenolysis and then, as glycogen runs out, by gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol and amino acids. The brain depends on glucose in the fed state but adapts to ketone bodies in prolonged starvation, which reduces the glucose that has to be synthesised from protein.
